checks.t: Checked which subscription you are in before changing anything
checks.why: The name Sandbox-Unit42 confirms you are in the subscription you were approved to use. Check first, then change.

checks.t: Switched the vault to the Azure RBAC permission model
checks.why: RBAC is the recommended model. It lets you give narrow data roles, scope them as tightly as one secret, and audit them like other role assignments.
Purge protection stops anyone, even an Owner, from permanently deleting soft-deleted items until the retention period ends. It also cannot be turned off again.

checks.t: Set the firewall default action to Deny
checks.why: With the default action set to Deny, only listed networks and the trusted-services exception can reach the vault. Public traffic from anywhere no longer can.

checks.t: Gave the app identity the Key Vault Secrets User role
checks.why: This role lets the identity read secret values and nothing else, which is least privilege for an app that only reads.

checks.t: Did not give the app a broad role or access policy
checks.why: Administrator, Owner or Contributor, or an access policy that allows delete and purge, gives the app far more than it needs and would make a stolen identity much more dangerous.

checks.t: Did not delete or purge the vault or touch kv-prod-shared
checks.why: Deleting the vault undoes the task, and changing another team's vault is outside the written approval.

q.title: Replace open RDP with Bastion and JIT
q.scenario: A test Windows VM in the unit's Azure subscription has a public IP and an NSG rule that allows RDP from anywhere. You have written approval to move admin access to Azure Bastion and just-in-time access. Add the steps in a safe order. Some ideas do not belong. Add only the steps that belong, in the order they should happen.
q.ticket: Change CHG-4402: VM vm-test01 in the unit's own subscription. Admin access must never be lost during the change. JIT is for any non-Bastion path.

rules.text: Enable Defender for Servers Plan 2 on the subscription
rules.why: Just-in-time VM access is a Plan 2 feature, so the plan has to be on before JIT can be configured.

rules.text: Deploy Azure Bastion in the AzureBastionSubnet of the VNet
rules.why: Bastion gives browser-based RDP and SSH over TLS without exposing the VM's own management ports.

rules.text: Test an admin session to the VM through Bastion
rules.why: Prove the new path works before taking the old one away, so you cannot lock yourself out.

rules.text: Enable JIT access for the VM for the management ports, with a short maximum request time
rules.why: JIT adds deny rules for the management ports and opens them only for an approved source and time. Existing allow rules on those ports still win, so the broad allow must also go (step e).

rules.text: Remove the VM's public IP and the broad RDP allow rule
rules.why: Once Bastion works, the public exposure serves no purpose and removing it shrinks the attack surface. Then reconnect through Bastion to confirm.

rules.text: Add an NSG rule that allows TCP 3389 only from the AzureBastionSubnet range, at a higher priority than the JIT deny rule
rules.why: Bastion connects over the VM's private IP. Once the broad allow is gone, JIT's deny rule would block it, so this narrow allow must outrank the deny. If you add it before JIT, JIT keeps it above its deny. If you add it after, give it a lower priority number than the deny.

rules.text: Open RDP from any address in the NSG at priority 100 so admins are never blocked
rules.why: This keeps the exposure you are trying to remove, and a priority 100 allow would also outrank later deny rules.

rules.text: Put the local administrator password in the ticket so the team can find it
rules.why: Passwords in tickets are readable by many people and break accountability. Use a vault or Entra sign-in.

rules.text: Turn off Defender for Servers on the subscription to save cost
rules.why: This removes the very plan that JIT depends on.

before.why: JIT needs Defender for Servers Plan 2 first, so the plan comes before the JIT setup.
Bastion has to exist before you can test a session through it.
Do not remove the old path until the new one is proven.
Prove the Bastion path works before you start locking down the management ports.
Keep Bastion working before the broad allow is removed, so admin access is never lost.

last.why: Removing the public IP and the allow rule is the one step that cannot be taken back easily, so it comes last, after everything else works.

q.title: Place the parts of a hub-and-spoke network
q.scenario: The unit is building a small hub-and-spoke network in its own subscription. A spoke VNet runs the app VMs and a database. Place each part in the right spot. Three parts in the tray do not belong.
q.ticket: Design review NET-12. Rules: all outbound traffic from the spoke is inspected centrally, admins reach VMs without public IPs, the database has no public path, and only the web tier may reach the app tier.

slots.label: Spot A
slots.hint: central filter for outbound and east-west traffic

slots.label: Spot B
slots.hint: admin RDP and SSH over TLS, no public IP on VMs

slots.label: Spot C
slots.hint: sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the filter's private IP

slots.label: Spot D
slots.hint: port rules that follow VM tiers as they scale

slots.label: Spot E
slots.hint: private IP in the VNet for the PaaS database

devs.name: Azure Firewall
devs.why: Azure Firewall in the hub inspects and filters traffic from the spokes, with rules by FQDN, address and port.

devs.name: Azure Bastion
devs.why: Bastion in its own subnet gives admins RDP and SSH through the browser, so VMs need no public IP.

devs.name: User-defined route to firewall
devs.why: A route table on the spoke subnet sends the default route to the firewall's private IP, so traffic cannot skip inspection.

devs.name: NSG using ASGs
devs.why: An NSG with application security groups allows web to app and denies the rest, and it follows VMs as they scale.

devs.name: Private endpoint for the database
devs.why: A private endpoint gives the database a private IP inside the VNet, so it needs no public path.

devs.name: Public IP on each app VM
devs.why: Public IPs expose each VM to the internet. Bastion removes the need for them.

devs.name: NSG rule: allow any, priority 100
devs.why: A broad allow at a high priority defeats the tier rules and the firewall.

devs.name: Storage key in the app config
devs.why: A stored key is a secret that can leak. Use a managed identity with a role instead.

q.title: Bring Linux logins into Sentinel and respond
q.scenario: The SOC wants SSH failures from a Linux forwarder in the unit's own Azure subscription to raise incidents in Microsoft Sentinel, with a Teams notice sent automatically. You have written approval from the workspace owner. Add the steps in a sensible order. Some ideas do not belong. Add only the steps that belong, in order.
q.ticket: Request SOC-88: new Syslog source. Use the existing resource group. Keep the playbook's rights as narrow as possible.

rules.text: Create a Log Analytics workspace and onboard Microsoft Sentinel to it
rules.why: Everything else needs a workspace with Sentinel turned on.

rules.text: Install the Syslog via AMA solution from the content hub
rules.why: The content hub solution brings in the data connector, so you can set up collection with Azure Monitor Agent.

rules.text: Create a data collection rule for the facilities and levels you need, and assign it to the forwarder
rules.why: The DCR tells Azure Monitor Agent what to collect and where to send it. Collecting only what you need also controls cost.

rules.text: Query the Syslog table to confirm events are arriving
rules.why: Check that data really lands before building detections on it.

rules.text: Create a scheduled analytics rule that raises an incident after repeated SSH failures
rules.why: The analytics rule turns raw events into an incident that analysts and automation can act on.

rules.text: Create an automation rule that runs the Teams playbook when that incident is created
rules.why: The automation rule links the incident to the playbook. The Sentinel service also needs the Automation Contributor role on the playbook's resource group.

rules.text: Install the retired Log Analytics agent (MMA) because it is simpler
rules.why: The legacy agent has been retired. Azure Monitor Agent with a DCR is the supported way.

rules.text: Give the playbook's identity Owner on the whole subscription
rules.why: Owner at subscription scope is far more than a Teams message needs. Grant only what the playbook uses.

rules.text: Collect every facility at every severity from every system just in case
rules.why: Collecting everything raises ingestion cost and drowns real signals. Collect what a detection needs.

rules.text: Create the Teams Logic Apps playbook with an incident trigger and a narrowly scoped managed identity
rules.why: The playbook has to exist before an automation rule can run it, and a narrow identity keeps its rights small.

before.why: The workspace with Sentinel must exist before you can install a solution into it.
The connector from the solution is where you create the data collection rule.
There is nothing to verify until collection is configured.
Confirm data first, then write a detection that depends on it.
The automation rule fires on incidents the analytics rule creates, so the rule comes first.
The automation rule needs an existing playbook to run.
